s0201.literal: How much more with the general's territory, the general's talent, the general's name, and the general's power—yet able to cultivate the fief in full, face north and call himself subject: could he speak of his achievements in the same year as Liu Ze?
s0201.idiomatic: With your territory, talent, name, and power, if you could truly keep your fief in order and face north as a subject, could your achievement be named in the same breath as Liu Ze's?

s0202.literal: Would not body and rivers-and-mountains share equal peace, and name and metal-and-stone wear out together?
s0202.idiomatic: Would not your person share the peace of the realm and your name endure like bronze and stone?

s0203.literal: I wish you would add thrice-over thought and consider it without neglect.
s0203.idiomatic: Please think it over again and again and do not overlook it.

s0204.literal: Ji—his vital force is thin and slight, his remaining shade has little left; grateful for grace and cherishing virtue, he does not notice his wild words; execution by axe and yue, he would find sweet as shepherd's purse.
s0204.idiomatic: My strength is failing and little time remains; grateful for your kindness, I speak rashly without thinking. If the axe falls on me, I shall take it as gladly as shepherd's purse.

s0205.literal: Baoying, reading the letter, was greatly angry.
s0205.idiomatic: Baoying read the letter and flew into a rage.

s0206.literal: Someone said to Baoying: "Lord Yu's illness grows daily worse; his words are mostly mistaken and absurd.
s0206.idiomatic: Someone told Baoying, "Lord Yu's illness is worsening; his words are mostly confused.

s0208.literal: Also because Ji had the people's regard, he moreover treated him with forbearance.
s0208.idiomatic: Also because Ji enjoyed public esteem, he treated him with forbearance.

s0209.literal: When Baoying was defeated and fled, at night he reached Putian, turned and said to his son Han Qin: "Had we early followed Lord Yu's plan, we would not have come to today.
s0209.idiomatic: When Baoying was defeated and fled, he reached Putian by night and said to his son Han Qin, "Had we followed Lord Yu's counsel sooner, we would not be here today.

s0210.literal: " Han Qin only wept, that was all.

s0211.literal: When Baoying was captured, of all the guests who had the slightest connection, all were put to death; only Ji, because of prior acquaintance, escaped calamity.
s0211.idiomatic: When Baoying was taken, every guest who had had dealings with him was executed; only Ji, through prior acquaintance, escaped.

s0212.literal: Initially the monk Huibiao ranged widely and had talent and thought; when Baoying raised troops, he composed a five-character poem to send him off, saying: "Sending horses still by the water, parting banners slightly catch the wind; behold tonight's moon—it should enter the Purple Forbidden Palace.
s0212.idiomatic: Earlier the monk Huibiao was widely read and clever. When Baoying took up arms, Huibiao sent him a five-character poem: "Horses still water the parting stream; banners catch the wind; see how tonight's moon should enter the Purple Forbidden Palace.

s0213.literal: " Baoying, obtaining it, was very pleased.

s0214.literal: Huibiao brought it to show Ji; Ji read it once and stopped, with stern countenance and no words.
s0214.idiomatic: Huibiao showed it to Ji. Ji read it once, set it down, and said nothing, his face stern.

s0215.literal: Huibiao withdrew; Ji said to those close to him: "Master Biao began with this—he will end with this.
s0215.idiomatic: When Huibiao left, Ji told his intimates, "Master Biao began with this; he will end with this.

s0216.literal: " Later he was indeed executed on this account.
s0216.idiomatic: " In the end he was executed for it.

s0217.literal: Emperor Wen soon ordered Area Commander Zhang Zhaoda to arrange his dismissal and send Ji back to court.
s0217.idiomatic: Emperor Wen soon ordered Area Commander Zhang Zhaoda to send Ji home to court.

s0218.literal: When he arrived, that very day he was granted audience; he said to Ji: "Guan Ning is unharmed.
s0218.idiomatic: On arrival he was received that same day. The emperor said to Ji, "Guan Ning is well.

s0219.literal: His mind to comfort and reward was like this.
s0219.idiomatic: Such was his warmth in greeting him.

s0220.literal: Before long Emperor Wen said to Dao Zhongju: "The Prince of Hengyang has left the inner quarters; though he has not yet been given palace staff, yet there must be one man to pass the day with him morning and evening and also keep the records—I should seek an elder scholar of established conduct.
s0220.idiomatic: Soon Emperor Wen told Dao Zhongju, "Prince Hengyang has left the inner palace. Though he has no staff yet, he needs someone with him day and night who can also keep his records. We should find a senior man of real conduct.

s0221.literal: " Zhongju did not know how to answer; the emperor said: "I have already found him.
s0221.idiomatic: " Zhongju had no answer. The emperor said, "I already have the man.

s0222.literal: " Thereupon by hand-edict he employed Ji.
s0222.idiomatic: " He then appointed Ji by personal edict.

s0223.literal: Ji entered to give thanks; the emperor said: "The reason I temporarily bend you to roam the fief is not only to trouble you with documents—it is also to have you serve him as teacher and model.
s0223.idiomatic: Ji came to give thanks. The emperor said, "I bend you to the prince's household not only for paperwork but to be his teacher and example.

s0224.literal: " Soon he was concurrently made Regular Attendant of the Scattered Cavalry; as envoy to Qi, Ji declined on grounds of age and illness and did not go; he was made Doctor of the National University.
s0224.idiomatic: " He was soon made regular attendant of the scattered cavalry and sent as envoy to Qi, but Ji pleaded age and illness and did not go; he was made doctor of the national university.

s0225.literal: Before long he also memorialized requesting to leave office and return to his home village; the emperor answered with a gracious edict and permitted him to go east.
s0225.idiomatic: Before long he memorialized to resign and return home; the emperor answered graciously and let him go east.

s0226.literal: He was then made Vice-Prefect of East Yangzhou; Ji again declined on grounds of illness.
s0226.idiomatic: He was then made vice-prefect of East Yangzhou; Ji again pleaded illness.

s0227.literal: When Emperor Gao Zong succeeded, he was summoned and appointed Yangzhou Administrator-in-Chief and Left Vice Director of the Masters of Writing, but he did not accept either post.
s0227.idiomatic: When Emperor Gao Zong succeeded, he was summoned as Yangzhou administrator-in-chief and left vice director of the masters of writing, but accepted neither.

s0228.literal: He was then made Adviser to the Eastern Palace General of the Prince of Jian'an, with the added title General Who Displays Martial Prestige; again he declined on grounds of illness, unable to attend morning and evening in the train.
s0228.idiomatic: He was then made adviser to the prince of Jian'an, eastern palace general, with the added title general who displays martial prestige, but again pleaded illness and could not attend daily.

s0229.literal: The prince therefore specially ordered a halt to princely-house business; when there were doubtful points, Ji was consulted to decide them—only on the first and fifteenth of the month did he draft the routine memorial.
s0229.idiomatic: The prince then stopped routine palace business for him; doubtful matters were referred to Ji for decision; he only drafted the regular memorial on the first and fifteenth of the month.

s0230.literal: In the eighth year of Taijian he was advanced to Grand Master of Palace Counsel; his general's title was unchanged.
s0230.idiomatic: In Taijian year 8 he was advanced to grand master of palace counsel, retaining his general's title.

s0231.literal: In the eleventh year he died, aged seventy.
s0231.idiomatic: In year 11 he died, aged seventy.

s0232.literal: From youth Ji was devoted in conduct; even in haste he was always generous and mild; though servants and boys he never addressed with harsh voice or color; yet when facing peril and holding to integrity, then his words and spirit were stern and cold, and he did not fear bare blades.
s0232.idiomatic: From youth Ji was steadfast in conduct; even in haste he was gentle and never raised his voice at servants or boys; yet in danger he held firm, his words icy, and he did not flinch from naked blades.

s0233.literal: From the time he was cast adrift in the southern lands, separated from his elder brother Li by a barrier, he therefore suffered from qi illness; whenever he received a letter from Li, his qi would rush into violent fits, and several times he was at the brink of death.
s0233.idiomatic: After he was stranded in the south, cut off from his brother Li, he suffered from a breathing disorder; each letter from Li brought on violent fits and several times nearly killed him.

s0234.literal: In every office he held, he never reached the full term; only a year or several months, and he would himself request to resign and withdraw.
s0234.idiomatic: In every post he never served a full term; after a year or a few months he would ask to resign.

s0235.literal: He often said: "Knowing sufficiency brings no disgrace—I know sufficiency.
s0235.idiomatic: He often said, "Knowing when one has enough avoids disgrace—and I have enough.

s0236.literal: " When he took leave for illness in his private home, whenever a prince was made area commander, on descending from his carriage he would always come to the gate with ritual; Ji was ordered to set aside whip and tablet and sit with a armrest and staff.
s0236.idiomatic: " In retirement at home, whenever a prince became area commander and alighted from his carriage, he came to Ji's gate with full ceremony; Ji was told to lay aside whip and writing board and receive him seated with staff and armrest.

s0237.literal: When he often went out to visit nearby temples, the lanes and hamlets would pass word to one another; old and young lined the roads, looking up and bowing on the left of the way.
s0237.idiomatic: When he went to nearby temples, neighbors spread word; old and young lined the road and bowed as he passed.

s0238.literal: Some who swore oaths as pledges would only point to Ji and not deceive—such was the reach of his supreme conduct.
s0238.idiomatic: Men who swore oaths would point to Ji and keep their word—such was the force of his conduct.

s0239.literal: The writings he composed, in the disorders were mostly not preserved.
s0239.idiomatic: Most of what he wrote was lost in the disorders.

s0240.literal: Ma Shu, styled Yaoli, was a native of Mei in Fufeng.
s0240.idiomatic: Ma Shu, styled Yaoli, was from Mei in Fufeng.

s0241.literal: His grandfather Lingqing was a Recorder in the Prince of Jingling's household under Qi.
s0241.idiomatic: His grandfather Lingqing had been recorder in the household of the prince of Jingling under Qi.

s0242.literal: When Shu was several years old both parents died; he was reared by his paternal aunt.
s0242.idiomatic: Shu lost both parents as a small child and was raised by his father's sister.

s0243.literal: At age six he could recite the Classic of Filial Piety, the Analects, and the Laozi.
s0243.idiomatic: At six he could recite the Classic of Filial Piety, the Analects, and the Laozi.

s0244.literal: When grown, he ranged to the limit through the classics and histories, and was especially skilled in Buddhist sutras and the meaning of the Changes and the Laozi.
s0244.idiomatic: Grown up, he was deeply read in the classics and histories and especially skilled in Buddhist sutras and the exegesis of the Changes and Laozi.

s0245.literal: Liang's Prince of Shaoling Xiao Lun was Inspector of South Xuzhou; having long heard his name, he summoned him as academician.
s0245.idiomatic: Xiao Lun, prince of Shaoling, was inspector of South Xuzhou; he had long heard of Shu and made him an academician.

s0246.literal: Lun at the time himself lectured on the Great Perfection Sutra and had Shu lecture on the Vimalakirti, the Laozi, and the Changes, setting topics the same day; clergy and laity who listened numbered two thousand.
s0246.idiomatic: Lun then lectured on the Great Perfection Sutra himself and had Shu lecture on the Vimalakirti, Laozi, and Changes the same day; two thousand clergy and laymen listened.

s0247.literal: The prince wished to observe fully the superior and inferior; he therefore said to the assembly: "In disputation with Academician Ma, you must make him yield—do not stand empty as guest and host.
s0247.idiomatic: The prince wished to test who was stronger and told the crowd, "In debate with Academician Ma you must make him yield; do not leave guest and host empty.

s0248.literal: " Thereupon several families of scholars each rose to pose questions; Shu then in sequence analyzed and judged, opening their main points, then branching into streams and divisions, turning and changing without end; the debaters bowed in silence and only listened—Lun greatly praised him.
s0248.idiomatic: " Several schools of scholars each raised questions. Shu answered in turn, opened each main point, then branched into endless distinctions; the debaters bowed and listened in silence. Lun was greatly pleased.

s0249.literal: Lun wished to recommend him to the court.
s0249.idiomatic: Lun meant to recommend him at court.

s0250.literal: Soon he encountered Hou Jing's rebellion; Lun raised troops to aid the Terrace City and left twenty thousand scrolls of books entrusted to Shu.
s0250.idiomatic: Soon came Hou Jing's rebellion. Lun raised troops to aid the capital and left twenty thousand scrolls with Shu.

s0251.literal: Shu with full intent searched and read them, nearly covering all; he then sighed and said: "I have heard that those who prize rank and title take Chao and Jufu as fetters, and those who love mountains and forests take Yi and Lü as granary keepers; binding name and reality makes Zhuangzi's words mere hay; playing with emptiness and purity makes seat-side doctrines mere chaff; checked against earnest discourse, each also follows his own preference.
s0251.idiomatic: Shu read through them almost entirely and sighed: "I hear that men who prize office take Chao and Jufu as shackles, and men who love the hills take Yi and Lü as storekeepers; those who bind name to fact treat Zhuangzi as straw, and those who play at emptiness treat banquet talk as chaff. In earnest judgment each follows his own bent.

s0252.literal: Yet Zhi Fu had the manner of yielding the kingship, and Yan Zi had the plan of defying the emperor—thousand-year fine tales that are not abandoned.
s0252.idiomatic: Yet Zhi Fu refused the throne, and Yan Zi defied his ruler—tales a thousand years old that are not forgotten.

s0253.literal: Compared with seekers of resolve today, they gaze at the road and cease.
s0253.idiomatic: Beside men who seek resolve today, they stop at the roadside and turn back.

s0254.literal: Is it that Heaven does not favor the lofty, or why are the hills and forests so little heard of?
s0254.idiomatic: Does Heaven not favor the high-minded, or why are recluses so seldom heard of?

s0255.literal: " He then hid on Mount Mao, with the will to end his days there.
s0255.idiomatic: " He then retired to Mount Mao, intending to end his days there.

s0256.literal: In the first year of Tianjia, Emperor Wen summoned him as Director of Revenue; he declined and did not answer the command.
s0256.idiomatic: In Tianjia year 1 Emperor Wen summoned him as director of revenue; he declined and did not answer.

s0257.literal: At that time Shu's kin and old friends all dwelt at Jingkou; each year at the turn of autumn and winter he would go to visit them.
s0257.idiomatic: His kin and friends then lived at Jingkou; each autumn and winter he visited them.

s0258.literal: When the Prince of Poyang was Inspector of South Xuzhou, admiring his loftiness and despising his inability to summon him, he therefore used humble words and thick kindness, ordering envoys to invite him—several times back and forth—yet Shu firmly declined on grounds of illness.
s0258.idiomatic: When the prince of Poyang was inspector of South Xuzhou, he admired Shu's loftiness but could not summon him; he used humble words and rich courtesy and sent envoys again and again, but Shu firmly pleaded illness.

s0259.literal: A disciple advanced and said: "The Prince of Poyang treats you as teacher and friend—it is not about rank; amid market and court, what harm in keeping silence?
s0259.idiomatic: A disciple urged him, "The prince of Poyang treats you as teacher and friend, not for rank. What harm in quiet presence amid court and market?

s0260.literal: " Shu, having no way out, then went.
s0260.idiomatic: " Shu, unable to refuse further, went.

s0261.literal: The prince separately built a chamber to house him; Shu hated its grandeur and splendor and therefore in the bamboo grove built his own thatched hut to dwell in.
s0261.idiomatic: The prince built him a separate house; Shu disliked its splendor and made a thatched hut in the bamboo grove.

s0262.literal: Whenever princes and dukes sent gifts, of those he could not decline, he generally accepted one part in ten.
s0262.idiomatic: When princes sent gifts he could not refuse, he usually took one part in ten.

s0263.literal: Shu from youth belonged to times of disorder; in every place he dwelt, bandits did not enter; those who relied on him were often several hundred households.
s0263.idiomatic: From youth Shu lived in disorder; wherever he stayed bandits did not enter, and hundreds of households often sheltered under him.

s0264.literal: His eye pupils were penetrating yellow and could see objects in the dark.
s0264.idiomatic: His pupils were bright yellow and could see in the dark.

s0265.literal: There were always a pair of white swallows that nested in the courtyard trees, tame on the eaves and verandas, sometimes perching on tables and desks; they came in spring and left in autumn—for nearly thirty years.
s0265.idiomatic: A pair of white swallows always nested in his courtyard trees, tame on eaves and verandas and sometimes on his desk; spring after spring and autumn after autumn—for nearly thirty years.

s0266.literal: In the thirteenth year of Taijian he died, aged sixty.
s0266.idiomatic: In Taijian year 13 he died, aged sixty.

s0267.literal: He composed Treatise on the Awakening of the Way in twenty scrolls, circulating in the world.
s0267.idiomatic: He wrote Treatise on the Awakening of the Way in twenty scrolls, which circulated in his time.

s0268.literal: The historiographer says: Shen Jiong served the Liang house; in years he had reached knowing fate—he hoped for thin posts in the secretariat, [13] and stopped at the low office of district magistrate; when he set brush to the alliance altar and composed words for exhortation and memorial, rousing and lifting the aim and tone—truly a great man among men of letters!
s0268.idiomatic: The historiographer says: Shen Jiong served Liang. Past knowing fate he had hoped for a modest secretariat post [13] and rose no higher than district magistrate; yet at the alliance altar and in memorial prose his voice soared—truly a great writer.

s0269.literal: Yu Li's presenting stratagems was deep and close, exhausting his sincere good faith—one may say he benefited the enlightened age.
s0269.idiomatic: Yu Li's counsel was deep and thorough and his loyalty complete—he truly served a bright age.

s0271.literal: Shen Jiong, styled Liming—"Liming" in the History of the Southern Dynasties reads "Chuming."
s0271.idiomatic: On "Shen Jiong, styled Liming": the History of the Southern Dynasties reads Chuming.

s0272.literal: Wang Mingsheng's Examination of Discrepancies among the Seventeen Histories cites He Zhuo's view, saying that to read "Liming" is correct.
s0272.idiomatic: Wang Mingsheng's Examination of Discrepancies among the Seventeen Histories cites He Zhuo: Liming is correct.

s0275.literal: [site]—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.
s0275.idiomatic: On "[site]": emended per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.

s0277.literal: [hundred] deaths, light on life—changed according to the Southern Supervisory edition and the Comprehensive Mirror 754.
s0277.idiomatic: On "[hundred] deaths, light on life": emended per the Southern Supervisory edition and Comprehensive Mirror 754.

s0278.literal: If he himself impaired his person in ritual—"ritual" in all editions reads "body"; the Comprehensive Mirror 754 is the same.
s0278.idiomatic: On "if he himself impaired his person in ritual": all editions read body; Comprehensive Mirror 754 agrees.

s0279.literal: Comment: this refers to the ritual one should keep toward one's own person; to read "ritual" is correct.
s0279.idiomatic: This refers to ritual owed one's own person; ritual is correct.

s0280.literal: Recently reason was urgent at leaning on the gate—"leaning on the gate" in the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions reads "leaning on the lane."
s0280.idiomatic: On "recently reason was urgent at leaning on the gate": Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions read leaning on the lane.

s0281.literal: Comment: both leaning on the gate and leaning on the lane speak of a parent's keen longing for a son; both appear in the Strategies of Qi in the Intrigues of the Warring States.
s0281.idiomatic: Both leaning on the gate and leaning on the lane mean a parent's longing for a son; both appear in the Qi strategies in the Intrigues of the Warring States.

s0284.literal: [pare] traces in hill and garden—changed according to the Southern Supervisory, Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.
s0284.idiomatic: On "[pare] traces in hill and garden": emended per the Southern Supervisory, Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.

s0285.literal: It was not Heaven alone—"not" was originally an ink dot in the base text and is now supplied from the various editions.
s0285.idiomatic: On "it was not Heaven alone": fei was faded in the base text and is restored from other editions.

s0286.literal: At first crossing difficulty—"difficult" was originally an ink dot in the base text and is now supplied from the various editions.
s0286.idiomatic: On "at first crossing difficulty": jian was faded in the base text and is restored from other editions.

s0287.literal: Weeping exhausted, blood followed—below "exhausted" the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions have the character "and."
s0287.idiomatic: On "weeping exhausted, blood followed": Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions add er after jin.

s0288.literal: By the years of one's birth—"by" in the Southern Supervisory reads "still."
s0288.idiomatic: On "by the years of one's birth": the Southern Supervisory reads still.

s0289.literal: Comment: you and you are interchangeable.

s0292.literal: [inherit] foundation—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions and the History of the Southern Dynasties and Comprehensive Mirror 832.
s0292.idiomatic: On "[inherit] foundation": emended per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions, the History of the Southern Dynasties, and Comprehensive Mirror 832.

s0295.literal: [Right] Canal—changed according to the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.
s0295.idiomatic: On "[Right] Canal": emended per the Northern Supervisory, Ji, and Hall editions.

s0296.literal: Comment: Right Canal was king of Korea in Western Han times.
s0296.idiomatic: Right Canal was a king of Korea in Western Han.

s0297.literal: Hoped for thin posts in the secretariat—"post" was originally erroneous as "office"; the various editions are not erroneous; it is now corrected.
s0297.idiomatic: On "hoped for thin posts in the secretariat": guan was miswritten huan in the base text; other editions read correctly; now emended.
